props.title: The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid
props.initialSlug: Outlaws vs. Town in Historic Bank Heist Gone Wrong

sections.content: The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid represents a pivotal shift in Western filmmaking, arriving during the revisionist era that gave us The Wild Bunch (1969) and McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971). Director Philip Kaufman strips away the romantic mythology of the James-Younger gang, presenting Robert Duvall's Jesse James as a dangerous religious fanatic rather than the folk hero portrayed in earlier films like Jesse James (1939). Cliff Robertson's Cole Younger emerges as the film's conscience - a pragmatic outlaw watching his way of life vanish as industrialization creeps across the frontier.

sections.content: Kaufman's attention to historical detail sets this film apart from previous James-Younger dramatizations. The actual 1876 Northfield raid marked the end of the post-Civil War outlaw era, and Kaufman captures both the violence and the absurdity of these Confederate veterans struggling against the march of progress. The film's depiction of the town's defense, with citizens using new repeating rifles against the raiders, emphasizes how technology was making the traditional outlaw obsolete.

The film bridges classic and modern Western sensibilities, maintaining period authenticity while incorporating contemporary themes about violence and social change. Like Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969), it shows outlaws confronting their own extinction, but without the earlier film's romantic gloss. Kaufman's approach influenced later revisionist Westerns like The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (2007) and The Long Riders (1980). sections.content: The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid marks a crucial evolution in how Hollywood portrayed historical outlaws. Earlier films like The True Story of Jesse James (1957) presented simplified good-versus-evil narratives, while Kaufman's film explores the complex social and economic forces that created and ultimately destroyed the outlaw bands. This more nuanced approach influenced later films like The Missouri Breaks (1976) and American Outlaws (2001), though few achieved Kaufman's level of historical authenticity.
